facts.title: Protocol — diplomatic usage
facts.text: Protocol refers to formal rules and procedures governing official or diplomatic conduct and events.

facts.title: State of emergency — bounded definition
facts.text: A state of emergency is an exceptional legal condition in which a government invokes special powers under applicable law; its content and safeguards vary by jurisdiction.

facts.title: Impeachment — constitutional process
facts.text: Impeachment is a constitutional process by which a legislature may bring formal charges against a public official; procedure and consequences vary by jurisdiction.

facts.title: Straw vote — definition
facts.text: A straw vote is a nonbinding, informal vote used to gauge opinion rather than make a final decision.

facts.title: Mesopotamia — between the rivers
facts.text: The name Mesopotamia means ‘between the rivers’; ancient Mesopotamia lay largely in what is now Iraq, with Babylon on the Euphrates River.

facts.title: Cuneiform — Mesopotamian writing
facts.text: Writing began in southern Mesopotamia before 3100 BCE; cuneiform developed from pictograms and was used by several ancient Mesopotamian cultures.

facts.title: Ziggurat — religious structure
facts.text: A ziggurat was a tall, stepped religious structure built in major ancient Mesopotamian cities.

facts.title: Hammurapi — Babylonian king
facts.text: Hammurapi became king of Babylon around 1792 BCE and ruled until about 1750 BCE.

facts.title: Hammurapi’s law-code
facts.text: Hammurapi’s law-code included laws based on older Sumerian laws and expressed standardized justice across the Babylonian empire.

facts.title: Neo-Babylonian empire — chronology
facts.text: The Neo-Babylonian empire lasted from 625 to 539 BCE; Nebuchadnezzar II reigned from 605 to 562 BCE and rebuilt/enlarged Babylon.

facts.title: Ashurbanipal — Neo-Assyrian king
facts.text: Ashurbanipal was king of the Neo-Assyrian empire from 669 to about 631 BCE and developed a large library of cuneiform tablets at Nineveh.

facts.title: Egyptian civil calendar
facts.text: Ancient Egypt’s civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days, with five additional epagomenal days at the end of the year.

facts.title: Ancient Egyptian day
facts.text: The Egyptian daily cycle was divided into 24 hours: 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night.

facts.title: Nile flood and calendar context
facts.text: Ancient Egyptian New Year was associated with the heliacal rising of Sopdet/Sirius and the first signs of the annual Nile flood.

notes.title: Political-label boundary
notes.text: Third World, communism, imperialism, Marxism, fifth column, xenophobia, satellite state, and Cold War labels are historically and politically context-dependent. They are not imported as unqualified current descriptions.

notes.title: Institutional-definition boundary
notes.text: Task force, junta, bureaucracy, dominion, and welfare-state descriptions depend on legal, historical, and institutional context. Only bounded definitions are retained; country classifications are withheld.

notes.title: Mesopotamian superlative boundary
notes.text: The scan’s ‘oldest civilization’, ‘first wheel’, and ‘first law’ claims are not imported as absolute facts. Ancient evidence and terminology require specific archaeological scope.

notes.title: Babylonian and Assyrian scope boundary
notes.text: The scan’s claims about first maps, first calendars, first iron weapons, and universal military labels are withheld. The Hanging Gardens attribution is treated as legend rather than fact.

notes.title: Egyptian origin and superlative boundary
notes.text: First-pharaoh, first-monotheism, exact unification, ‘largest’, and causal claims are withheld unless exact source support is available. Approved records remain archaeology-based and historically scoped.
